notes: Permission to appeal refused on contracted-out deduction under PSA section 46; statutory text is clear.

enrichment.short_title: Pearce v DWP: contracted-out deduction from SERPS additional pension

statutes_considered.title: Social Security Contributions and Benefits Act 1992

key_facts: Ms Pearce claimed her State retirement pension from February 2002 was underpaid by about £40 per week.
She had a contracted-out guaranteed minimum pension (GMP) of £57.40 revalued from £15.56 when she left the Exxon Mobil scheme in 1984.
The DWP deducted the full revalued GMP from her pre-1997 additional SERPS pension despite later contracted-in employment.
The Social Security Commissioners upheld the deduction; she sought permission to appeal to the Court of Appeal.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for permission to appeal from a Social Security Commissioner decision refusing permission to appeal on State pension calculation.
enrichment.outcome: Permission to appeal refused; Lloyd LJ held section 46(1) clearly required deduction of the lesser of pre-1997 additional pension or the revalued GMP for the whole payment period.
enrichment.ratio: Under PSA section 46(1) the contracted-out deduction applies to the weekly Category A pension for the period it is in payment and is the lesser of pre-1997 additional pension or the GMP at its revalued amount, without limiting deduction to contracted-out periods or the original GMP figure.
legal_issues: Whether section 46(1) 'any period' refers only to contracted-out employment years
Whether only the unrevalued GMP (£15.56) may be deducted rather than the revalued amount
Interaction between GMP preservation legislation and the State pension contracted-out deduction
Whether DWP guidance inconsistent with the statutory scheme affects construction

notes: Tracing/election abuse of process appeal; permission granted on dismissal but refused on plant amendments.

enrichment.short_title: De Crittenden v Bayliss estate: tracing claim after damages election
key_facts: De Crittenden claimed half the proceeds of a 1997 Lloyds Bank compromise with Charles Bayliss under an alleged profit-sharing agreement.
Judge Nicholl awarded £37,000 damages in a first action for breach of contract in 2001, which was fully enforced.
A second action sought a proprietary tracing remedy into Carlton Mews property allegedly funded from the £75,000 compromise payment.
Judge Kirkham refused late re-amendments and dismissed the second claim as an abuse of process and for lack of fiduciary duties.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Applications for permission to appeal against refusal of re-amendment and dismissal of a second Chancery tracing claim.
enrichment.outcome: Permission to appeal granted against the dismissal order; amendment on paragraph 14 adjourned to the substantive appeal; permission refused on plant-related amendments.
enrichment.ratio: Election to pursue damages for breach of contract and successful enforcement may bar a later proprietary tracing claim arising from the same transaction, but election/abuse of process and fiduciary duty issues on the facts merit full Court of Appeal consideration.
legal_issues: Whether late amendment to plead use of the full £75,000 was properly refused
Whether the second action was an abuse of process after damages were chosen and enforced
Whether Bayliss owed fiduciary duties supporting a tracing claim
Whether plant items never charged to the Bank could support the agreement claim

notes: Bad character applications under CJA 2003; Bovell and Dowds convictions held safe.

enrichment.short_title: R v Bovell and Dowds: Criminal Justice Act 2003 bad character

statutes_considered.title: Criminal Procedure and Investigation Act 1996
provisions: Part II Code of Practice paragraph 5.8

key_facts: Bovell was convicted of wounding with intent after stabbing a shopkeeper; the defence sought to adduce the complainant's decade-old robbery conviction under section 100.
Post-trial disclosure revealed the complainant had carried a knife in the 1993 robbery and faced an unprosecuted 2001 section 18 allegation unknown at trial.
Dowds was convicted of burglary; after attacking his co-accused's character in evidence, the Recorder admitted his two prior burglary convictions under section 101.
Both applications followed R v Hanson, Pickstone and Gilmore on bad character notice and admissibility.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Full Court applications for leave to appeal against conviction on bad character rulings under the Criminal Justice Act 2003.
enrichment.outcome: Both applications dismissed; Bovell's conviction safe despite possible different ruling on robbery with knife; Dowds' section 101(3) fairness discretion correctly exercised.
enrichment.ratio: Late disclosure of complainant bad character may not render a conviction unsafe where independent witness evidence is strong and defendant bad character would inevitably have been adduced; section 101(3) fairness does not require investigating a defendant's motive for attacking another's character.
legal_issues: Admissibility of complainant's old convictions under section 100(1)(b)
Whether unprosecuted 2001 wounding allegation is section 100 evidence
Fairness under section 101(3) after a section 101(1)(g) character attack
Retention of CPIA material for bad character proceedings
linked_authorities: R v Hanson, Pickstone and Gilmore [2005] EWCA Crim 824

notes: GDC erasure appeal; Collins J dismissed challenge to sanction on postponed and new misconduct proceedings.

enrichment.short_title: Hossack v GDC: erasure after postponed and new dental misconduct
key_facts: Dr Hossack faced old GDC proceedings in 2001 for unpaid laboratory bills and record-keeping failures, with sanction postponed.
New 2004 proceedings concerned seriously deficient treatment of four patients and lack of professional indemnity insurance.
The Committee erased him from the register under rule 16(2) simultaneously disposing of old and new charges.
Mitigation showed partial improvement since postponement but reports questioned his proactive compliance and insight.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal under section 29 of the Dentists Act 1984 against GDC Professional Conduct Committee erasure.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; erasure upheld as a decision the court could not say was wrong given serious clinical misconduct and incomplete remediation.
enrichment.ratio: Under GDC rules 11(2) and 16(2) past misconduct found in postponed proceedings may be considered with new charges when determining serious professional misconduct and sanction; mitigation since postponement does not require detailed rejection in reasons where seriousness of proved facts is overwhelming.
legal_issues: Construction of GDC rules 11(2) and 16(2) on simultaneous disposal
Whether legal assessor advice improperly separated mitigation from sanction
Distinction between culpability for misconduct and penalty mitigation after Campbell v GMC
Adequacy of Committee reasons for rejecting mitigation and ordering erasure
linked_authorities: Campbell v General Medical Council [2005] EWCA Civ 250
Silver v General Medical Council [2003] UKPC 33

notes: Green Belt gypsy site s288 challenge failed; Inspector's very special circumstances finding not Wednesbury unreasonable.

enrichment.short_title: Mole Valley v SoS: Green Belt private gypsy site permission
key_facts: Henry Smith, a gypsy, applied to use land at the Evergreens, Ryegate Road as a private gypsy site in Mole Valley Green Belt.
The council refused permission; an Inspector allowed the appeal finding very special circumstances under PPG2.
Mr Smith had lived on the site as a child, bought the field from his father, and had acute accommodation needs with no realistic alternatives.
Mole Valley challenged the decision as perverse, arguing gypsy site shortfall across the south-east was too commonplace to be very special.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Section 288(1)(b) statutory challenge to quash a planning Inspector's grant of Green Belt change-of-use permission.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; the Inspector's balancing exercise and finding of very special circumstances was not objectively unreasonable.
enrichment.ratio: A regional shortage of gypsy sites does not prevent an individual's acute personal need and lack of alternatives from being, in aggregate, very special circumstances outweighing Green Belt harm; widespread similar problems do not negate objectively special circumstances for one applicant.
legal_issues: Whether the Inspector's very special circumstances finding was Wednesbury unreasonable
Application of PPG2 paragraphs 3.1-3.2 balancing test
Whether personal accommodation need can be very special in a context of regional site shortfall
Relevance of R (Chelmsford) v SoS (Draper) and Basildon v SoS
linked_authorities: R (Chelmsford Borough Council) v First Secretary of State (Draper) [2003] EWHC 2978
Basildon District Council v First Secretary of State [2004] EWHC 2759

notes: Case stated on alibi; magistrates irrationally treated identification proof as separate from disproving alibi.

enrichment.short_title: DPP v Kipling: flawed magistrates' alibi burden reasoning
key_facts: A 17-year-old complainant was indecently assaulted near Airy Hill School, Whitby; she and witness Cheryl Cook identified Kipling.
Kipling and his mother gave alibi evidence that he was collected and taken to a barber around the time of the offence.
Youth Court justices believed the identification evidence but acquitted because the prosecution had not separately rebutted the alibi to their satisfaction.
The case was stated asking whether dismissal was correct despite belief in identification and the offence.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by way of case stated from Scarborough Youth Court acquittal on indecent assault.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; matter remitted with direction to convict because satisfied identification necessarily disproved the alibi.
enrichment.ratio: Where magistrates are sure of identification and that the defendant committed the offence, the Crown has necessarily disproved an alibi; it is irrational to treat rebutting credible alibi evidence as an additional burden separate from proof of guilt.
legal_issues: Whether the prosecution bears a continuing separate burden to rebut alibi after proof of identity
Correct model directions on alibi and identification in magistrates' courts
Appropriate remedy on case stated: direction to convict versus retrial

confidence.notes: Short, definitive case stated with clear irrationality finding and remittal order.

notes: Guidance on relisting absent sentence appeals; Spruce and Anwar reductions confirmed.

enrichment.short_title: R v Spruce and Anwar: relisting absent sentence appeals
key_facts: Spruce received 4 years for distributing indecent images of children; the Full Court reduced it to 3.5 years in his absence on renewal.
Anwar's flat-related sentences were reduced from 7 years to 3 years consecutive to a 16-year term, totalling 20 rather than 23 years.
Both sought relisting after absent hearings; Spruce relied on an updated GP report about his wife's multiple sclerosis.
The court considered when absent defendants may relist and what fresh material justifies rehearing.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Relisted Full Court hearings following in-absentia sentence reductions on renewed applications for leave to appeal.
enrichment.outcome: Guidance given on relisting practice; neither appellant obtained further reduction—Spruce at 3.5 years and Anwar at 20 years total.
enrichment.ratio: An appellant has a section 22 right to be present at the appeal hearing but relisting after an absent successful renewal requires fresh material with important bearing on sentence; counsel should obtain instructions to proceed in absence and 'do better' letters should normally go only to unrepresented defendants.
legal_issues: Scope of section 22(1) right to be present at sentence appeals
When to relist after in-absentia sentence reduction
What fresh material warrants full rehearing versus comment on earlier judgment
Whether a differently constituted court might increase sentence on relisting
linked_authorities: R v Oliver [2003] 1 Cr App R 463

confidence.notes: Explicit practice guidance plus case-specific confirmation of prior reductions.

notes: Unsafe conviction; judge wrongly excluded cross-examination on prior false complaints under section 41.

enrichment.short_title: R v Garaxo: section 41 and previous false complaint cross-examination

statutes_considered.title: Youth Justice and Criminal Evidence Act 1999

key_facts: Garaxo was convicted of sexual assault and common assault on a woman he met on Shepherd's Bush Green after sharing drink.
The defence sought to cross-examine the complainant on two earlier CRIS reports of assault allegations she did not pursue in 2000 and 2001.
The trial judge refused cross-examination under section 41, finding insufficient basis to show the prior complaints were untrue.
The Crown also adduced a prior robbery complaint about a prostitute without a Lucas direction.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against conviction by leave of the Single Judge on bad character and previous complaint rulings.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; convictions quashed and retrial directed despite appellant having served nearly all of the original sentence.
enrichment.ratio: Cross-examination on prior complaints capable of showing fabrication is not necessarily section 41 sexual behaviour evidence; where there is a proper evidential basis under R v T & H that prior complaints were made and may be untrue, the judge must permit the questioning.
legal_issues: Whether prior false complaint cross-examination is caught by section 41
Proper evidential basis for alleging previous complaints were untrue
Admissibility and Lucas direction for prior inconsistent prostitute complaint evidence
Whether retrial is appropriate after substantial time served

confidence.notes: Clear unsafe conviction finding on section 41 ruling with retrial ordered.

notes: Probate trial; Second Will admitted in solemn form after capacity and knowledge findings.

enrichment.short_title: McClintock v Calderwood: testamentary capacity in care home
key_facts: Dr Joseph McClintock signed two wills in January 1999 leaving his estate to his niece-in-law Sandra Calderwood while resident at St Ives Lodge care home.
Probate of the First Will (19 January) had been granted to Dr Calderwood; the Second Will (22 January) appointed her executor.
Brother Eric McClintock challenged both wills for lack of testamentary capacity and want of knowledge and approval.
Medical evidence showed fluctuating confusion possibly linked to medication, but solicitors and care staff described coherent dealings when instructions were given.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Chancery trial to revoke probate of the First Will and admit the Second Will to probate in solemn form.
enrichment.outcome: Second Will admitted to probate in solemn form; probate of the First Will revoked; court satisfied Dr McClintock had capacity and knew and approved both wills.
enrichment.ratio: Fluctuating confusion in a care home resident does not negate testamentary capacity if, on the evidence at the time instructions were given, the testator understood the nature and effect of dispositions favouring his closest carer; surprising benevolence to a niece-in-law does not alone undermine capacity.
legal_issues: Whether Dr McClintock had testamentary capacity in January 1999
Whether he knew and approved the contents of each will
Effect of fluctuating confusion and medication on capacity
Which will was last and should be admitted to probate

notes: Family second appeal largely refused; permission granted on inherent jurisdiction power of arrest defect.

enrichment.short_title: Re M-B: care, freeing and injunction appeals
key_facts: Mrs MD, mother of five Hackney children, challenged care orders, freeing for adoption of the youngest, and High Court injunctions against harassing carers.
Final care orders and freeing of baby I for adoption were upheld by Ryder J and HH Judge Horowitz QC after extensive fact-finding.
Ex parte inherent jurisdiction injunctions with powers of arrest were obtained to protect foster and family placements.
The mother applied for permission to appeal twelve orders, acting in person.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Single Lord Justice of Appeal hearing multiple applications for permission to appeal in consolidated family proceedings.
enrichment.outcome: Permission refused on care, freeing and most procedural orders as second appeal or spent directions; permission granted on challenge to powers of arrest attached to inherent jurisdiction injunctions.
enrichment.ratio: A second appeal from the Family Division under AJA 1999 section 55(1) requires an important point of principle or compelling reason and will not reopen routine care findings; a power of arrest cannot be attached to an order made under the court's inherent jurisdiction.
legal_issues: Whether section 55(1) bars a second appeal against Ryder J's dismissal of IL&CFPC appeals
Propriety of freeing the youngest child for adoption and dispensing with consent
Whether ex parte inherent jurisdiction injunctions required return dates
Jurisdiction to attach powers of arrest to inherent jurisdiction orders
linked_authorities: Re G (Wardship) (Jurisdiction: Power of Arrest) (1983) 4 FLR 538
Harrison and Another v Lewis; R v S [1988] 2 FLR 339
